blocks.title: Getting information
blocks.content:
INTERFACES;ip a;nmcli device show;—
GATEWAY;ip route | grep default;nmcli device show | grep GATEWAY;—
ROUTES;ip route;nmcli device show | grep IP4.route;—
DNS;resolvectl status;nmcli device show | grep IP4.DNS;cat /etc/resolv.conf
HOSTNAME;hostnamectl;nmcli general hostname;cat /etc/hostname
blocks.footer:
ip is instantaneous (ip addr add, ip route add); nmcli (nmcli con mod) and netplan apply stays after reboot; ip don't.
ADVANCED: To see actual routes table, use: cat /proc/net/route

blocks.title: Basic diagnostics
blocks.intro: Lost in the troubleshooting? Start from the ground up — check each layer before moving to the next.
blocks.content:
INTERFACE UP AND HAS IP?;ip a
DO I REACH ROUTER?;ping -c 4 <gateway ip>
DO I REACH INTERNET?;ping 8.8.8.8
IS DNS SOLVING?;dig example.com (nslookup example.com)
EVERYTHING IS OK?;ping google.com

blocks.title: SETTING PROPERTIES
blocks.content:
ACTIVATE/RESTART INTERFACE;ip link set eth0 up | down;nmcli con up | down eth0
STATIC IP/MASK;ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0;nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24
REMOVE IP;ip addr del 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0;nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses ""
SETTING DHCP;dhclient eth0 (needs ISC dhclient);nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method auto|manual
GATEWAY;ip route add default via 192.168.1.1;nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1
ADD STATIC ROUTES;ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 192.168.1.254;nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.routes "10.0.0.0/24 192.168.1.254"
REMOVE ROUTES;ip route del 10.0.0.0/24;nmcli con mod eth0 -ipv4.routes "10.0.0.0/24 192.168.1.254"
DNS;resolvectl dns eth0 8.8.8.8;nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1"
DNS DOMAIN SEARCH;resolvectl domain eth0 example.com;nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.dns-search example.com
HOSTNAME;hostnamectl set-hostname new-name;nmcli general hostname new-name
APPLYING CHANGES;Immediatelly, but it's overwritten after reboot;nmcli con up eth0
blocks.footer:
ip: change the kernel state on time but doesn't persist after reboot.
nmcli: Write a connection profile, saving configuration after reboot (by NetworkManager).

blocks.title: How to find what is the active network manager
blocks.content:
To discover what is the network manager, use:

_sudo systemctl is-active NetworkManager_
_sudo systemctl is-active systemd-networkd_
_sudo systemctl is-active systemd-resolved_

blocks.title: NOTES
blocks.content:
Most commands here require root privileges — sudo was omitted in several places for readability.
Placeholders like <interface>, <ip>, <gateway> must be replaced with real values.

**{color:#c44815:This cheatsheet assumes a standard Debian setup with NetworkManager. Commands may vary slightly depending on your distro version or network manager in use.}**

blocks.title: Static IP - nmcli
blocks.footer: If the STATE of interface is unmanaged, try using netplan.
blocks.content:
# Use this command to discover the connection name (CONNECTION column).
# If the device STATE is unmanaged, read below.
sudo nmcli device
# If no connection exists yet, create one
sudo nmcli c add type ethernet con-name <name> ifname <interface>

sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.addresses <ip>/<mask>
sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.gateway <gateway>
sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.dns "<dns1> <dns2>"
sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.dns-search "domain.test"
sudo nmcli c down <name>
sudo nmcli c up <name>

# Confirm
nmcli device show <interface>

blocks.title: Static IP - NETPLAN
blocks.intro:
Netplan is the network declarative configuration layer, for NetworkManager or systemd-networkd.
Create a file in /etc/netplan/test.yml:
blocks.footer:
_Give permissions to all configuration files:_
sudo chown root:root /etc/netplan/*.yaml
sudo chmod 600 /etc/netplan/*.yaml
_Then to activate/restart interface, use netplan apply_
blocks.content:
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd  # or 'NetworkManager', depends on backend
  ethernets:
    eth0:
      dhcp4: false    # if true, ignores addresses/routes/gateway
      addresses:
        - 192.168.1.10/24        # IP/mask (CIDR)
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.168.1.1       # default gateway
        - to: 10.0.0.0/24
          via: 192.168.1.254     # additional static route
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1]   # DNS servers
        search: [exemplo.com]           # DNS search domain

blocks.title: DNS
blocks.intro: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
blocks.content:
ADD INDIVIDUAL HOST;echo "192.168.1.10 client.domain.test client" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
SET DNS SERVER;sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.dns 192.168.0.100
IGNORE AUTO DNS (DHCP);sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.ignore-auto-dns yes
SET DNS SEARCH DOMAIN;sudo nmcli c m <name> ipv4.dns-search "dominio.test"
APPLY CHANGES;sudo nmcli c down <name> && sudo nmcli c up <name>
FLUSH DNS CACHE (systemd-resolved);sudo resolvectl flush-caches
REAPPLY DNS (NetworkManager);sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager
blocks.footer:
To set DNS directly, edit _/etc/resolv.conf_
To lock _/etc/resolv.conf_ against NetworkManager overwrite: _sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf_

blocks.title: DNS Diagnotics
blocks.content:
What DNS server am I using?;resolvectl status;cat /etc/resolv.conf
Can I resolve this domain?;dig example.com;nslookup example.com
Does this specific DNS server work?;dig example.com @8.8.8.8;nslookup example.com 8.8.8.8
What domain does this IP belong to?;dig -x 8.8.8.8;nslookup 8.8.8.8
Is DNS slow?;dig example.com | grep "Query time";—
Just give me the IP;dig +short example.com;—
Where is resolution failing?;dig +trace example.com;—
What are the MX/NS/TXT records?;dig example.com MX;dig example.com NS
What does the system actually resolve?;getent hosts example.com;—

blocks.title: Setting Wi-fi with nmcli
blocks.footer:
To add another network to nmcli, use: _nmcli device wifi connect "<SSID2>" password "<PASS2>"_
This creates a new profile automatically. List all profiles with: _nmcli connection show_
blocks.content:
sudo nmcli radio wifi on                                # enable wifi radio
nmcli device set <interface> managed yes                # let NetworkManager manage
nmcli device wifi list                                  # scan/list networks
nmcli device wifi connect "<SSID>" password "<PASS>"    # connect
sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager                   # restart service

blocks.title: Wi-Fi via Netplan
blocks.footer: Apply with: netplan apply. If IP needs to be static, see how to do in Netplan static configuration example.
blocks.content:
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: NetworkManager        # wifi generally uses NetworkManager as backend
  wifis:
    wlan0:
      dhcp4: true                 # get IP via DHCP
      access-points:
        "SSID1":                  # add how many you wish
          password: "password1"

blocks.title: Setting Wi-Fi with IP / WPA Supplicant
blocks.content:
sudo ip link set wlan0 up                                             # enable interface
sudo iw dev wlan0 scan | grep SSID                                    # scan networks
wpa_passphrase "<SSID>" "<PASS>" | sudo tee /etc/wpa_supplicant.conf  # generate config 
sudo wpa_supplicant -B -i wlan0 -c /etc/wpa_supplicant.conf           # connect
sudo dhclient wlan0                                                   # get IP via DHCP

blocks.title: Wi-Fi Advanced Status
blocks.content:
NETWORKMANAGER LOGS;journalctl -u NetworkManager -f
AUTHENTICATION LOGS;journalctl -u wpa_supplicant -f
PCI CHIPSET/DRIVER;lspci -k | grep -A3 Network
USB CHIPSET;lsusb -v
DRIVER BOOT ERRORS;dmesg | grep -i wlan

blocks.title: Wi-Fi Troubleshooting
blocks.content:
Is the interface up?;ip link show wlan0;nmcli device status
Are there networks nearby?;nmcli device wifi list;iw dev wlan0 scan | grep SSID
What am I connected to?;nmcli device show wlan0;iw dev wlan0 link
Is the signal weak?;iwconfig wlan0;iw dev wlan0 station dump | grep signal
Am I getting an IP?;ip a show wlan0;nmcli device show wlan0 | grep IP4.ADDRESS
Can I reach the gateway?;ping -c 4 $(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $3}');—
Can I reach the internet?;ping -c 4 8.8.8.8;mtr 8.8.8.8
Is it a DNS problem?;dig exemplo.com;resolvectl status
What does the driver/hardware say?;dmesg | grep -i wlan;lspci -k | grep -A3 Network
What is NetworkManager doing?;journalctl -u NetworkManager -f;journalctl -u wpa_supplicant -f
blocks.footer: To install iwconfig and iw, use: _sudo apt install iw wireless-tools_

blocks.title: VLAN/bridge/bonding (virtual interfaces)
blocks.intro:
**VLAN** segments a physical network into isolated virtual networks using tagged interfaces.
**Bridge** connects multiple interfaces into a single logical network (common in VMs/containers).
**Bonding** aggregates multiple physical interfaces for redundancy or increased throughput.
blocks.content:
Create VLAN interface;sudo ip link add link eth0 name eth0.10 type vlan id 10
Create bridge;sudo ip link add br0 type bridge
Add interface to bridge;sudo ip link set eth0 master br0
Create bonding (link aggregation);sudo modprobe bonding && sudo ip link add bond0 type bond
List VLAN/bridge interfaces;ip -d link show

blocks.title: ARP
blocks.intro: ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local network. The kernel keeps this mapping cached — checking or editing it helps troubleshoot local connectivity and detect spoofing.
blocks.content:
Local ARP table (known IP↔MAC);ip neigh;arp -a
Find MAC of a specific IP;ip neigh show to <ip>;arp -n <ip>
Add static ARP entry;ip neigh add <ip> lladdr <macaddress> dev <interface>;—
Delete/flush ARP entry;ip neigh flush to <ip>;—
blocks.footer: To use arp, install: _sudo apt install net-tools_

blocks.title: SS & NETSTAT
blocks.intro: See what's connected, listening, or waiting — ss shows active sockets and connections, useful for spotting open ports, established sessions, or unexpected traffic.
blocks.content:
List all active connections;ss -tun;netstat -tun
Show connections with process;sudo ss -tulnp;sudo netstat -tulnp
Count connections by state;ss -antH | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c;—
Show only established connections;ss -t state established;netstat -t | grep ESTABLISHED
Show only listening ports;ss -tuln;netstat -tuln
Filter by port;ss -tuln | grep :443;netstat -tuln | grep :443
Show connections to a specific IP;ss dst 192.168.1.10;netstat -tn | grep 192.168.1.10
blocks.footer: To use netstat, install: _sudo apt install net-tools_

blocks.title: Proxy
blocks.intro: A proxy sits between your machine and the internet, forwarding requests on your behalf — often used to bypass restrictions, cache traffic, or route through a specific network.
blocks.content:
Set proxy for current shell session;export http_proxy="http://proxy:3128";export https_proxy="http://proxy:3128"
Set for apt;echo 'Acquire::http::Proxy "http://proxy:3128"\;' | sudo tee /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/95proxy;—
Set system-wide proxy (persistent);edit /etc/environment → add http_proxy=...;—
Check proxy env vars;env | grep -i proxy;printenv | grep -i proxy
Test if proxy is being used;curl -v https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -i proxy;—
Bypass proxy for specific hosts;export no_proxy="localhost,127.0.0.1,.local";—

blocks.title: Network Troubleshooting
blocks.content:
IS THERE ANY CONNECTIVITY AT ALL?;ping -c 4 8.8.8.8;PORT SEEMS CLOSED BUT SERVICE IS RUNNING?;sudo ss -tulnp | grep <PORT>
SEE DEFAULT GATEWAY;ip route | grep default;TRAFFIC ISN'T REACHING A SERVICE?;sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port <PORT>
CHECK IF GATEWAY RESPONDS;ping -c 4 $(ip route | grep default | awk '{print $3}');FIREWALL BLOCKING OUTBOUND TRAFFIC?;sudo iptables -L OUTPUT -n -v
TEST WEBSITE ACCESS;curl -I https://example.com;NAT/MASQUERADE NOT WORKING?;sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v
TEST THROUGH PROXY;curl -x http://proxy:3128 -I https://example.com;VM/CONTAINER HAS NO NETWORK?;ip -d link show
TRACE ROUTE TO HOST (HOP BY HOP);traceroute 8.8.8.8;HIGH LATENCY OR PACKET LOSS?;sudo iftop -i eth0
TRACE + LATENCY PER HOP;mtr -rw 8.8.8.8;BANDWIDTH HOG ON THE NETWORK?;sudo iftop -i eth0

blocks.title: Firewall/NAT
blocks.intro:
**FIREWALL:** Filters network traffic based on rules (allow/deny/reject) by port, protocol, IP, or interface, protecting the system from unwanted connections.
**NAT:** Translates IP addresses/ports between networks — commonly used to share one public IP among multiple internal hosts (masquerade) or route traffic to internal services.
**IPTABLES:** Low-level Linux firewall tool managing netfilter tables directly (filter, nat, mangle). More flexible but verbose syntax; rules aren't persistent by default.
**UFW:** Simplified frontend for iptables. Enables/disables the firewall, sets default policies, adds rules by port/protocol/IP/interface, supports rate limiting and app profiles — rules persist automatically.
blocks.content:
List rules;sudo iptables -L -n -v / sudo nft list ruleset;sudo ufw status verbose
Allow a port;sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT;sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
Block an IP;sudo iptables -A INPUT -s 1.2.3.4 -j DROP;sudo ufw deny from 1.2.3.4
Allow traffic on specific interface (ports 80/443);sudo iptables -A INPUT -i eth0 -p tcp -m multiport --dports 80,443 -j ACCEPT;sudo ufw allow in on eth0 to any port 80,443 proto tcp
NAT/masquerade (share internet);sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE;edit /etc/ufw/before.rules manually
Save rules persistently;sudo netfilter-persistent save;automatic (ufw enable persists)
Enable firewall;—;sudo ufw enable
Remove a rule;sudo iptables -D INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT;sudo ufw delete allow 22/tcp

blocks.title: Network Hardening
blocks.content:
Default deny incoming (for whitelist);sudo ufw default deny incoming
Allow only needed ports (for whitelist);sudo ufw allow 22,80,443/tcp
Restrict access by interface;sudo ufw allow in on eth0 to any port 80,443 proto tcp
Restrict access by source IP;sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24
Rate-limit SSH connections;sudo ufw limit ssh
Disable unused network protocols;blacklist in /etc/modprobe.d/ (e.g. dccp, sctp)
Lock /etc/resolv.conf against overwrite;sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf
Use trusted DNS servers only;set nameservers via nmcli/netplan (avoid ISP default)
Disable IP forwarding (if not router);net.ipv4.ip_forward=0
Enable SYN flood protection;net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1
Disable ICMP redirects;net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
Ignore broadcast pings;net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts=1

blocks.title: Other Hardening (not covered here)
blocks.intro: See other types of hardening not covered on this cheatsheet:
blocks.content:
Disable unused services;Reduces attack surface — a stopped service can't be exploited.
Restrict sudo access;Fewer root-capable users means fewer ways to compromise the whole system.
Enable AppArmor/SELinux;Confines processes, limiting damage even if one is compromised.
Use Fail2ban;Bans IPs automatically after repeated failed login attempts.
Use 2FA (Google Authenticator PAM);Second layer of verification — a leaked password/key alone isn't enough.
Set account lockout policies (pam_tally2/faillock);Blocks accounts after repeated failed logins, slowing brute-force.
Monitor ports (ss/nmap);Detects unexpected services or backdoors.
Centralize logs (rsyslog, Wazuh);Keeps logs safe even if the server is compromised.
Use VPN (WireGuard/OpenVPN) for admin access;Keeps SSH/panels off the public internet.
Segment network (VLANs/firewalls);Limits lateral movement from a compromised host.

blocks.title: Network Scanning
blocks.intro: Network scanning helps you discover what's alive on a network, which ports are open, and what services are running — useful for inventory, troubleshooting, and security audits. nmap is the standard tool for this, but there are faster/simpler alternatives depending on the goal: arp-scan and netdiscover work at Layer 2 (fast, local network only), while nmap works at Layer 3+ (routable, more detailed, but slower). Always scan networks you own or have permission to scan.
blocks.content:
Is a specific host alive?;ping -c 4 192.168.1.10
Discover hosts on local network (Layer 2, fast);sudo arp-scan --localnet
Discover hosts on a subnet (no ports);sudo nmap -sn 172.16.38.0/23
List only IPs that are up, sorted;sudo nmap -sn -n 172.16.38.0/23 -oG - | awk '/Status: Up/ {print $2}' | sort -V
Count total hosts found;sudo nmap -sn -n 172.16.38.0/23 -oG - | awk '/Status: Up/ {print $2}' | sort -V | awk 'BEGIN{c=0} {print\; c++} END{print "Total hosts:", c}'
Scan common ports on a single host;nmap 192.168.1.10
Scan specific ports across a subnet;sudo nmap -n -p 22,80 172.16.38.0/23
List hosts with specific ports open, sorted + counted;sudo nmap -n -p 22,80 172.16.38.0/23 -oG - | awk '/Status: Up/ {print $2}' | sort -V | awk 'BEGIN{c=0} {print\; c++} END{print "Total hosts:", c}'
Identify service/version on open ports;nmap -sV 192.168.1.10
Detect OS of target;sudo nmap -O 192.168.1.10
Full aggressive scan (OS+version+scripts+traceroute);sudo nmap -A 192.168.1.10
Fast scan of a large range;sudo masscan -p22,80,443 172.16.38.0/23 --rate=1000
blocks.footer: To use arp-scan and netdiscover, use: sudo apt install arp-scan netdiscover masscan.

blocks.title: TCPDUMP (packet capture)
blocks.intro: Tcpdump captures and inspects network packets in real time, using filters by host, port, or protocol.
blocks.content:
Capture on an interface;sudo tcpdump -i eth0
Capture with more detail;sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -v
Filter by host;sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.10
Filter by port;sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 443
Save capture to file;sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap
Read saved capture;tcpdump -r capture.pcap
blocks.footer:
To use tcpdump (if not installed), use:
_sudo apt install tcpdump_

blocks.title: Agressive Scans | ARP spoofing | MITM
blocks.content:
Script scan (vulns);nmap --script vuln <ip>
Banner grabbing (identify service);nmap -sV --version-intensity 5 <ip>
Stealth scan (SYN, evade logging);nmap -sS <ip>
Evade firewall (fragment packets);nmap -f <ip>
Spoof source IP;nmap -S <fake-ip> <ip>
Common vulnerable ports;nmap -p 445,3389,21,23 <ip>/<mask>
Detect ARP spoofing;arpwatch -i eth0 
Perform ARP spoofing (audit);sudo arpspoof -i eth0 -t <target-ip> <gateway-ip>
Sniff credentials (auth);sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 80 or port 21 -A
blocks.footer:
To use arpwatch and arpspoof, install:
_sudo apt install arpwatch dsniff_

blocks.title: WI-FI AUDITING HANDSHAKE CAPTURE
blocks.content:
Enable monitor mode;sudo airmon-ng start wlan0
Disable monitor mode;sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon
Scan nearby networks;sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon
Target specific BSSID/Channel;sudo airodump-ng --bssid <BSSID> -c <channel> wlan0mon
Capture handshake to file;sudo airodump-ng -c <channel> --bssid <BSSID> -w capture wlan0mon
Verify handshake in pcap;tshark -r capture-01.cap -Y "eapol"
Deauth test (audit client);sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a <BSSID> -c <CLIENT_MAC> wlan0mon
blocks.footer:
To use airmon-ng, airodump-ng, aireplay-ng, and tshark, install:
_sudo apt install aircrack-ng tshark_
